# Assignment 1

## Data (Part 1)

The data is imported and partitioned 50/50 between the training/testing data
using the procedure in the slides.
Relevant data for the task is extracted (Sample 1..100, Fat) for both
training and testing data:

```{r extract-data, echo=TRUE}
```

## Modeling Linear Regression (Part 1)

The imported data is used to train a linear regression model that predicts
Fat based on Sample 1..100:

```{r fit-lm, echo=TRUE}
```

```{r calculate-mse}
```

To get an indication on the quality of the model, the MSE is calculated:

```{r print-mse, echo=TRUE}
```

### Comments (Part 1)
The MSE for the test data is much higher than the MSE for the training data.
The model is extremely overfit, hence it makes bad predictions for unseen data.
There are too many features compared to the number of
samples (108 samples for training with 100 features).

### Underlying Probabilistic Model (Part 1)

The underlying probabilistic model for the linear regression
for the entry i is as follow:

$$
y_i = \theta_0 + \theta_1 x_{i1} + \cdots + \theta_{100} x_{i100} + \varepsilon_i
$$
Where $\varepsilon$ corresponds to the error term.

## Modelling LASSO (Part 2)

```{r training-function, message=FALSE}
```

A LASSO model is trained using a custom training function. It returns a glmnet
model and takes the training data and alpha (0 for Ridge, 1 for LASSO) as
arguments.

```{r training-lasso, echo=TRUE}
```

### Cost Function (Part 2)

The cost function that should be optimized for this scenario is as follows:

$$
\frac{1}{n} \sum_{i=1}^n
(y_i - \theta_0 - \theta_1x_{1i} - \cdots - \theta_px_{pi})^2
+ \lambda \sum_{j=1}^p|\theta_j|
$$

Where *n* is the number of entries and *p* is the number of parameters and
*$\lambda$* represents the penalty factor.

### Plot (Part 3)

The following plot illustrates how the regression coefficients depend on the
log of the penalty factor.

```{r plot-lasso}
```

As can be seen from the plot, all coefficients have a value when the penalty
factor is close to zero. This closely reassembles a regular linear
regression model. As the penalty factor grows, the amount relevant features
shrink at different paces. When the penalty factor is high enough, all features
are zero.

### Deciding on a Model with Three Features (Part 3)

As can be seen from the previous plot, when the log of the penalty factor
is between -1 and 0, most of the features are zero. More precisely, two of the
final three features shrink to zero when the log of the penalty factor is
just below zero. This means that to get a model with exactly three features
in this case requires the log of the penalty factor to be just below zero
(and large enough to not incorporate four features).

## Modelling Ridge (Part 4)

The same training procedure applied on LASSO is repeated for Ridge.

```{r training-ridge, echo=TRUE}
```

### Plot (Part 4)

The following plot illustrates how the regression coefficients depend on the
log of the penalty factor.

```{r plot-ridge}
```

### Conclusions (Part 4)

By inspecting the graph, it is clear that Ridge spreads out the applied
penalty on all features, while LASSO picks them off one by one.
From this, one can conclude that LASSO is more efficient when one wants to
create a smaller subset of features, while Ridge is more effective when
the one wants to spread out the penalty effect across multiple features.

## Modelling LASSO with Cross-Validation (Part 5)

```{r cv-function}
```

A LASSO model is trained using a custom training function. It returns a
cv.glmnet model and takes the training data and
alpha (0 for Ridge, 1 for LASSO) as arguments.

```{r training-cv, echo=TRUE}
```

### Plot (Part 5)

The following plot illustrates the dependence of the CV score on log of
the penalty factor.

```{r plot-cv}
```

As can be seen from the plot, the MSE is steady for low penalty factors, but
starts to grow rapidly when the log of the penalty factor is between -2 and -1.
Around when the log of the penalty factor is around zero, the increase tapers
off and keeps on increasing but at a slower rate.

### Optimal Penalty Factor (Part 5)

As can be seen from the the plot, the optimal penalty factor is
represented by the leftmost dotted vertical line (where log of the penalty
factor is between -3 and -2, closer to -3).

The following code snippet reports the number of chosen variables:

```{r variables-chosen-cv, echo=TRUE}
```

As can be seen from the printout, the number of chosen variables for this
model is 8.

#### Does the information displayed in the plot suggests that the optimal penalty factor results in a statistically significantly better prediction than the log of the penalty factor = −4? (Part 5)

No. The MSE if actually a bit lower when the penalty factor is zero,
compared to the optimal penalty factor (the leftmost dotted vertical line in the
plot). This makes sense, because a very low penalty factor equates for a more
complex model that is well fit to the training data.
The MSE is still relatively low for the optimal penalty factor, even though it
has reduced the number of  features from 100 to 9. It should, in theory,
work good (or at least better compared to a penalty factor close to 0) on
unseen data.

### Original Test Values vs Predicted Test Values (Part 5)

The following scatter plot illustrates the original values from the test data
compared with the predicted test values from the LASSO model with a penalty
factor of 0.05744535.

```{r scatter}
```

As can be seen from the plot, the model predictions are generally in the 
right neighborhood. However, the squared error is still relatively high for
most values. From this, one can conclude that the model is not great, but it is
a drastic improvement from the linear regression model with a MSE of around
722.
